s: To brighten up — to become more cheerful; To take a shine to — to develop a liking for; To make hay when the sun shines — to make the most of an opportunity while it lasts; Come rain or shine — whatever the weather/situation; To chase rainbows — to pursue something impossible/impractical; To save for a rainy day — to put something aside for a future time of need; To wait for a raindrop in the drought — to wait/hope for something which has little chance of happening.

Right as rain — fit and healthy; To take a rain check — to refuse an offer while showing willingness to accept it later; Into each life some rain must fall — everyone must experience difficulties at some time; To rain on someone's parade — to spoil someone's plans; It never rains but it pours — misfortunes come all at once; Raining cats and dogs — raining heavily; Dry spell — a period of less success than usual; Windfall — a large amount of money unexpectedly received.

To shoot the breeze — to have a casual conversation; To get wind of something — to hear a rumour about something; To know which way the wind blows — to understand changing circumstances and anticipate what will happen; To sail close to the wind — to verge on the limit of what is acceptable; To throw caution to the wind — to take a great risk; Cloud/storm on the horizon — an approaching problem; Every dark cloud has a silver lining — every difficult situation has a hopeful aspect; Cloud nine — a state of great happiness; To have your head in the clouds — to have unrealistic or fanciful ideas; "I don't have the foggiest" — I have no idea.

shortQuestions: Earth's atmosphere blurs, absorbs and distorts light from space and blocks ultraviolet and infrared rays. A telescope above the atmosphere gets sharp, clear images and can see much fainter and more distant objects, so cosmologists placed Hubble in space.

Light takes time to travel; when we look at a distant star we see the light that left it long ago — thousands or even billions of years — so we are seeing the star as it was in the past, not as it is now. Looking at stars is like looking into history.

Because galaxies are mostly empty space: the distances between stars are so huge that when the Milky Way and Andromeda collide, the stars will pass by each other without crashing; the Sun and Earth will only drift to a new place in the merged galaxy, so life on Earth will not be disturbed.

The Hubble Deep Field is an image made by pointing Hubble at a tiny, apparently empty patch of sky for many days. It revealed thousands of very distant galaxies of different shapes and ages, showing the universe as it was billions of years ago.

In star nurseries (huge clouds of gas and dust), gravity pulls the gas together into dense clumps; as they shrink they heat up and form protostars. When the core becomes hot enough, nuclear fusion ignites and a new star is born, while the leftover material may form planets.

When an exoplanet passes in front of its star (transit), a little starlight passes through the planet's atmosphere. Each gas absorbs particular colours (wavelengths) of light, leaving a unique 'fingerprint' in the spectrum; by spectroscopy scientists read these fingerprints to know which gases (water vapour, methane, etc.) are present.

In astronomy the light we see is old and may be bent, dimmed or reddened on its way, and objects may have changed or no longer exist. Gravity can bend light (gravitational lensing), making objects appear in different places or shapes — so what we see is not always the true present state of the object.
activities: Sample essay — Old Means of Communication vs Modern Means of Communication (point-by-point): Introduction: Communication has always been a human need, but its means have changed greatly. Point 1 — Speed: In the past messages were carried by messengers, pigeons or letters that took days or weeks; whereas today e-mail, mobile phones and social media deliver messages in seconds. Point 2 — Reach: Old means were limited to nearby places; in contrast, modern means connect the whole world instantly. Point 3 — Cost and ease: Sending a messenger or letter was slow and costly; similarly, telegrams were expensive, but now messages are almost free and easy. Point 4 — Personal touch: However, old letters were personal and preserved as memories, while modern messages are quick but often casual. Conclusion: Modern means are faster and more convenient, yet we should keep the warmth and care of the old ways.

Guessing game guide: one student gets a secret word (e.g., 'sun') and explains it without saying it — "It rises in the east, gives us light and heat, and plants need it to make food." Others listen carefully and guess. The activity practises descriptive speaking and listening.
